In this way, the sensor can be removed easily after removing the cover and disconnecting the connector.

VE.N.I.C.E PLUS ELECTRICAL AND ELECTRONIC SYSTEM GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS In conventional electrical systems, functions are activated with the aid of dedicated point-to-point connections. As the number of eletrical/electronic devices on board new vehicles has increased, the connection are becoming more complex and heavy. One reason for this is the complexity of functions implemented in the many electronic units, which require a continual interchange of data. All this makes it more difficult to install new electrical systems and increases the complexity of fault diagnosis. Many problems have been resolved and new electrical systems have been optimised compared to conventional systems by means of networking. This provides a more effective means of managing communication on board the car and for the transfer of information between subsystems via the serial buses present: single wires, pairs of twisted wires or even optical fibres. VE.N.I.CE (VEHICLE NETWORK INTEGRATION COMPONENT ELECTRONICS) ARCHITECTURE This is an application of the tried and tested multiplexing or (MUX) system The VE.N.I.CE PLUS system optimises the electrical system because each control unit is located in the centre of the functions it manages. This allows minimisation of the power and signal distribution system through the extensive use of serial communication networks. Power distribution takes place through junction units connected to the control elements (relays, actuators etc.) to ensure the maximum electrical protection and the minimum wiring complexity. The wiring architecture is reduced because each system function requires fewer dedicated cables because the wires (ABS, airbag, sidebag) are built into the front, facia or rear wiring harness. This also makes installation easier. Systems of this type offer innumerable advantates; for example: sensors in the various subsystems are made available to the network; information may be shared; similar sensors can be done away with; system flexibilty is increased; new functions can be added only by modifying the software (developed during the vehicle life), wiring design is simplified and the number of connectors is reduced, electronic device operating safety is increased to improve the reliability of information transmited, an integrated diagnostic function simplifies service operations on electric/electronic components. Tx - information to be transmitted to the nodes A (A1,A2) B (B1, B2) C (C1, C2) Rx - information received from nodes (B1, B2, C1) B (A1, A2, C2) C (A2, B1, B2) Classic solution The three control units (electronic nodes) require a number (N) of wires for each input/output in order to perform their function. This has created so much wiring that the system is more complex (design and manufacture), more bulky (weight, bulk and cost) and requires some 40 kg of wiring harnesses amounting to a length of more than 2 km. This requirement is likely to double every 10 years because even now one such vehicle may be equipped with 20 to 40 control units (ECUs). The first step that allowed us to reduce the volume and the complexity of the wiring harnesses was to group several electronic functions in a single unit: fewer control units = fewer wires. Examples of integration The engine control unit (NCM) manages injection, ignition, pollution system and engine cooling etc. 1 - Engine management control unit 2 - Engine cooling fan- first speed 3 - Engine cooling fan - second speed 4 - Injectors (injection) 5 - Coils (ignition) 6 - Lambda probe The multifunction control unit that manages: front window operation, door lock/release, timed passenger compartment and boot lighting, heated rear window timed activation and door mirror demisters. 1 - Multifunction control unit 2 - Door lock/release control unit 3 - Electric window control unit 4 - Timed front courtesy lights 5 - Timed luggage compartment light 6 - Activation of door mirrors and heated rear window for timed demisting The integration of electrical/electronic functions in a single electronic unit (ECU) has allowed us to improve: power consumption management (lower battery usage); functionality of appliances because they are managed by a single control unit; fault diagnosis due to control unit self-diagnosis. This first stage has allowed us to reduce the number of electronic units but not to reduce the volume of wiring harnesses sufficiently. Multiplexing solution Involves exchanging information between different electronic units on a single transmission channel (principle already used for the phone network, radio, TV etc.): 1 BUS (2 wires) for all information A-B-C - Nodes (ECU) A1-A2-B1-B2-C1-C2 - Communication bus D - Body Computer master control unit This second stage allows a decisive improvement because: Wiring is simplified and reduced Number of sensors is reduced (sharing of information) Electronic units communicate with one another. Obviously, the greater the number of systems requiring interconnection , the more attractive the MULTIPLEXING solution appears In general, in order to send data via multiplexing, we need to define the following with precision: transmission channel (wires, optical fibres, radio waves etc.); signal type on the channel (voltage, current, light etc.); communication protocol (all the rules that allow management of analogue or digital transmission management, code type, address, transmission order, error recording etc.). On our cars, the transmission medium or channel is a pair of wires known as a BUS. Under this system, packages of information are transmitted one after another without a set rigid sequence but according to the control units' needs). The signals are generated as voltages and the protocol used is CAN (controller area network), a system Robert Bosch in 1983 and has been developing ever since. Can (controller area network) network structure To allow the exchange of information, electrical/electronic systems in VENICE PLUS communicate via two physically separate networks known as low speed B-CAN and high speed C-CAN. Data to be shared between the B-CAN and C-CAN networksare managed by the Body Computer which acts as a system gateway because it is equipped with both interfaces. Via this device, two different network architectures are able to connect and convert certain application protocols into equivalent protocols in the other system. In practice, the body computer transfers information from the B-CAN (low speed) network to the C-CAN (high speed) network through the gateway and viceversa. Transfer may take place in two ways: directly: i.e. the entire message is copied to the other network exactly as it is; fragmented: i.e. the message received is broken down into its fields (signals) and recomposed as a new message by the other network. Connection of low speed can (b-can) In order to transfer information, all the electrical/electronic units are connected to the network via integrated, compatible interfaces in order to receive and transmit data. The B-CAN network (low speed) may feature up to 10 nodes (one per each control unit), all connected via a wire pair (CAN BUS). Maximum BUS length must not exceed 20 m and transmission speed is 50 kbit/sec. The communciation interfaces built into the electronic units for receiving and transmitting data are known as transceivers. One fundamental requirement of C-CAN BUS wires is that they should be in plaited or twisted pairs. By winding two electrical wires into a plait or coil, the degee of immunity to electromagnetic interference of external origin is reduced. The ECUs in the two CAN networks are programmed and operate by storage, processing and transmission of data and information by means of a binary convention, i.e. two symbols that refer to two basic electrical states: absence of voltage or presence of voltage; i.e. open circuit or closed circuit; i.e. level (0) zero or level (1) one Levels (0) and (1) constitute the basic information unit and are known as a BIT (binary digit). Binary ECUs use a binary language compatible with their electronic circuits (high low) (open closed etc.): data must therefore be handled in accordance with particular codes in order to transmit data. Various codes have therefore been developed to meet all requirements. One of the most common is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange). This alphanumerical code uses coded groups of bits and can represent the 26 letters of the British alphabet, plus the ten decimal figures in addition to punctuation marks and commands. ASCII is an eight-bit binary code. Seven bits are used to codet the information and the eighth is used to control errors. Using seven bits per character it is possible to code no fewer than 128 information items including decimal numbers, upper and lower case letters of the alphabet, punctuation marks etc.Once the number of bits in a word (i.e. the word length), has been fixed by a data code, this number must not be changed. A group of eight bits is known as a byte and represents no fewer than 256 values: this number is obtained by considering all possible combinations of (0) and (1) in the eight available byte positions, e.g. 00000001, 00001111, 11111111 etc. The number 256 (2 exp. 8) allows us to consider a set of alphabetical characters, punctuation marks, accented characters or special characters etc. In essence, a single byte may represent a number, a letter of the alphabet, a punctuation mark or a special character. The byte is used as a unit of measurement to describe quantities of data stored and storage capacity of storage devices. As with units of measure, byte are also defined as multiples: 1 kilobyte (kb) = 1024 bytes = 2 exp. 10 (2 10 ) 1 megabyte (Mb) = 1024 kb (about one million bytes)= 2 exp. 20 (2 20 ) 1 gigabyte (Gb) = 1024 Mb (about one billion bytes) = 2 exp. 30 (2 30 ) 1 terabyte (Tb) = 1024 Gb (about one trillion bytes) = 2 exp. 40 (2 40 ) Analogue: So-called linear electronics concerns analogue effects, i.e. that are proportional, continuous. A water tap is an example of an analogue switch because it can be used to shut off the water supply completely or turn it on fully, but can also be adjusted to all possible intermediate positions within the continuous range between closed and fully open states. The Tester mobile coil instrument is analogue: the needle can indicate the measurement position from zero to full scale deflection and also pass continuously along the graduated scale through all the points on its travel. It is often useful to determine a certain measurement by taking a value beween two marks on the scale within which the instrument pointer stops. Digital: A digital electronic system proceeds in discrete jumps, i.e. quantifiable steps. A light switch is an example of digital operation because it can only take up well-defined, distinct states. Two in this case: on and off, without intermediate positions. In practice, a digital gauge with warning lights or numbers proceeds in steps and it is not possible to determine, for example, the exact level of a liquid between the state when the warning light is on and the state when the level gauge warning light is of. The sensitivity is therefore of the step due to the interval between one warning light and another but the reading is precise and not subjective. It is possible to place a series of steps between one warning light and the next with the same number of lighted indicators - and so until the measurement is taken in such small steps that it is almost the same as the continuum measured by the analogue gauge. The similarity is more apparent than real because each step travelled by the digital indicator, however small, determines a well-defined position and an unequivocal value that is above all not subject to reading errors of parallax or interpolation. To sum up, the sensitivity of a digital instrument is unparalleled and the reading precision is much higher. OPERATION OF THE MULTIPLEX NETWORK (VE.N.I.CE PLUS SYSTEM) In the VeNICE architecture, the system designers made the Body Computer responsible for control functions. The additional Body Computer functions provide information on: network activity status; the functional failure status of individual node ECUs; CAN network failure. The Body Computer node 'wakes the system up' when the ignition key is turned to MAR. In the event of an NBC failure, the network is woken up by the Instrument panel node (NQS) which intervenes only if the system is not woken up by the Body Computer for a certain time after the key is turned to ON to prevent network conflicts. Each 'Node' ECU processes the various signals from the respective sensors for their management and that of the other ECUs. For greater clarity, the following drawings illustrates a possible data sharing procedure between units connected in a network. In the latest generation of electrical systems a very high number of electronic units can be interconnected and a very high number of packages can therefore be handled. For this reason, these systems use one or more CAN networks which allow better information exchange between the various electronic units compared with conventional wiring. The physical medium used for the B-CAN network (low transmission speed) is a double copper electrical wire (not necessarily plaited) while C-CAN networks (high transmission speed) require a plaited wire; with one of the two wires associated with the high level (H) and the other with the low level (L). The CAN bus signals are differential, i.e. the value assigned to each bit is represented by the different voltage of CAN (H) and CAN (L). The combined use of two cables and differential signals allows data packages to be exchanged beween the various control units via the CAN network, even in the presence of electromagnetic interference. Transmission and exchange of data on the B-CAN and C-CAN and the transfer of information between a low speed network and a high speed network and vice versa takes place in the body computer node (gateway function). The teeth (maximum flow) and gaps (minimum flow) on the engine pulley toothed ring gear pass continuously in front of an rpm sensor to set up an emf or variable voltage pulses as indicated theoretically in the figure. In order to be used by the ECU microprocessor, the analogue rpm sensor signals must be amplified if they are weak (when ring gear speed is low or when the number of teeth is low) and converted to digital signals by means of a trigger circuit. The binary counter counts them: one pulse for each tooth. To prevent the numbering from going on to infinity, a time signal (clock) consisting of a transistorised circuit governed by a quartz every second restores the count to zero in order to start again. If we know the number of teeth on the ring gear, we can obain the crankshaft rotating speed. If a crownwheel has 240 teeth and turns at a speed of 1000 rpm, in one second 1000 ( 240 : 60 = 4000 teeth will pass in front of the sensor corresponding to 4000 impulses. If a binary counter clocks up 40000 impulses (bits) in a second, the crankshaft speed must be 1000 rpm. The speed will be higher than 1000 if it clocks up more than 4000 bits. The rpm reduced to digital form is one of the many information items used by the microprocessor (7) in processing data; In practice, a program stored in the control unit memories is able to convert the processing results into signals that act as inputs to the work circuits: injection base pulse constant, current intensity and duration in the coil primary winding, injection operation or the supply of other actuators designed for different functions; since this signal is destined to be used by other nodes, the engine control unit makes it available on the C-CAN network via its CAN node. In practice, the control unit converts the rpm signal into binary numbers - the only type that can be used by the microprocessor. They are then relayed to the CAN controller (10), which prepares a data package made up of different blocks or fields (contained between a beginning and an end) and represents an entire series of information to be sent to other nodes. The other interface, i.e. the CAN transceiver (11), decodes the package and sends it on the BUS network. In practice, it receives a series of pulses known as bits of value one (1) zero (0) that determine dominant or recessive voltage levels throughout the time the node transmits. All the other nodes that receive the package correctly confirm the reception (acknowledgement) on the BUS. All receiving nodes also carry out a test to check that the package (message) is relevant to them. Any node that finds relevant data in a package accepts it and processes it. Otherwise it ignores it. Communication protocol The circulation of transmission of a message known as a data package (frame) on a multiplexing network (B-CAN and C-CAN network) is possible only if a transmission protocol is adopted. This set of rules allows the exchange of information and commands between two or more electric units (control units or more accurately nodes). In practice, the communication protocol defines the structure of a frame and a frame obviously consists of a series of pulses (known as bits) that take a value of one (1) or zero (0). FRAME FORMAT 1 - Frame 2 - Blocks A - Identifies the start of transmission or the beginning of a new frame (START OF FRAME) SOF) consists of 1 dominant bit and indicates to all other interfaced nodes to be synchronised to this SOF bit (wakes up any BUSES that may be in stand-by mode). B - Identifier marks and identifies the content of a message. Also contains all information on message recipients. Arbitrage of the transmitted frame is carried out on this field. This means that the identification code uniquely identifies frame content and the priority assigned to it by the network architecture. (the lower the identification number, the higher the priority) C - Control field indicates frame or message structure D - Data to be transmitted (may be orders or information for transmission) E - Control field; checks that data transmitted are not altered (message validity). The node or nodes that first detect the presence of an error emit a series of dominant notification bits, the transmitter node eliminates the message and emits a new frame after a certain time. F- Reception confirmation (Aknowledment). All receiving nodes that use the message and have recorded the correct sequence from the transmitter node (recessive bit) overwrite the recessive bit with a dominant bit. In this way, the transmitting node is assured of correct message reception by at least one recipient. Each node checks the frame that it is receiving. If it finds it relevant, it accepts it and processes it. Otherwise it ignores it. G - End of frame, message terminated. The end of frame allows (if no node begins a new transmission to the network (BUS)) the system to enter a state of inactivity (IDLE) Management of priorities (superimposing or collision of non-desctructive frame) The VE.N.I.CE system protocol can deal with problems of superimposition when several nodes wish to issue a frame simultaneously. Each control unit possesses an identification code that is also an expression of its priority. In practice, when a node (control unit) expresses its intention to send a frame on the network (BUS) by means of its intial bit and another node (control unit) does the same thing simultaneously, because both read network signals (as well as transmitting them), the node that finds a difference between the emitted signal and received signal can tell if the other node is emitting a higher priority frame. A node sending a lower priority message interrupts its transmission immediately to make way for the node transmitting a higher priority signal. In practice, the higher priority message is sent via the network without any interruption or delay. Naturally, the control units (nodes) that intended to send messages with lower priority and had to interrupt transmission to become receivers, resume transmission of their own frames when transmission is complete. This non-destructive superimposition is regulated by means of an arbitrage bit: one is known as the dominant bit and its value is zero (0). The other bit is said to be recessive and its value is equal to one (1). The Body Computer (NBC) activates the supply to the heated rear window if: an INT signal is present (ignition key on), the facia control button connected to the climate control system ECU (NCL) is pressed (button pressed signal is sent to the body computer (NBC) via the CAN network. Automatic rear window heater element operation is dependent on the engine rpm signal. The following activation/deactivation strategy is applied: For the first 10 minutes, operation does not depend on the engine speed The next 10 minutes are dependent on engine rpm Engine rpm lower than 950 rpm: the rear window should go off after 10 minutes Engine rpm higher than 950 rpm: heated rear window should go on or stay on if already activated until it has been effectively working for 20 minutes. It may be deactivated during this period of automatic operation only if battery voltage drops below 8.5 V ± 0.5 V. If the button on the facia is repressed for at least for at least 50 ms or if the key is turned off, the heated rear window is deactivated. Since rpm information from the engine control unit node (NCM) travels on the C-CAN network (high transmission speed) to reach the instrument panel node (NQS), which is connected to the B-CAN network (low transmission speed) it must be processed by the Body Computer (NBC) via the gateway function. Only after reprocessing does the body computer transfer the required information to the instrument panel node via the B-CAN network. (rev counter management) The interface between the engine control unit (NCM) and Selespeed control unit (NCR) is immediate because both are connected to the same CAN network. The other control units, which are not involved in the exchange of controls - e.g. the infotelematic or radio receiver node (NIT/NRR), that are in listening mode, read the information relayed down the BUS lines but do not process them because they are not essential for managing their functions. Braking system node frame 2 (nfr) vehicle speed (speedometer signal) The ABS control unit (NFR) is the transmitting node The receiving control unit are: Selespeed control unit (NQS), climate control sysem ECU (NCL), infotelematic/radio node (NIT/NRR) and Body Computer node (NBC). The instrument panel node (NQS) uses vehicle speed informtion or speedometer signal to control the speedometer pointer km/mile/hour and manage the odometer function (mileometer, trip counter). The Selespeed control unit (NCR) uses the speedometer signal because it is necessary and complementary to the engine rpm signal sent from the engine control unit (NCM) to manage gear shifts as comprehensively as possible. The climate control unit (NCL) also uses the speedometer information to manage outside temperature information that it receives from the relevant sensor located on the door mirror via the driver's door node (NPG). In other words, if car speed does not exceed 30 km/h, the outdoor air temperature value is updated only if it is lower than the value stored previously when the key was turned to 'MARCIA' position If car speed exceds 30 km/h for at least 1 minute, the outdoor temperature value replaces the previously stored value, whether it is lower or higher. The infotelematic node/radio node (NIT/NRR) uses vehicle speed information to manage sound intensity (radio volume) The manner in which data is sent between the transmitting control unit and the receiving control units is as described for the PREVIOUS FRAME. Serial line This dedicated serial line ensures data exchange between the various electronic units (nodes Essentially, the serial line is a copper wire used for consecutive data transmission by alternating high voltage levels (H) and low voltage levels (L) in continuation, i.e.serially. The figure above illustrates the High (H) and Low (L) voltage levels of the serial signal, i.e.: High (H) level: corresponds to a value higher than 80% of the battery voltage: logic level 1 Low (L) level: corresponds to a value lower than 20% of the battery voltage: logic level 0 Example: with a battery voltage of 12 V: High (H) level = > 9.6 V; Low (L) level = < 2.4 V. The data package communication protocol is defined by the baudrate, i.e. according to the number of bits (elementary message units) sent on the serial line in a second, i.e. baud rate The transmission speed is generally low (1000 baud rate = 10 kb/sec) Many information items are sent and mean response time is a few seconds. Control units connected to serial line k The control units connected to serial line K are shown below: 1 - Body Computer (NCM) front and rear view 2 - Air Bag Control Unit (CAB) 3 - ABS control unit (NFR) 4 - Selespeed control unit (NCR) 5 - Electronic injection control unit (NCM) 6 - Serial line K Control units connected to dedicated lines (serial) The control units connected to dedicated lines are shown below. 1 - Body Computer (NBC) 2 - Volumetric sensor control unit (CAV) 3 - Antitheft siren control unit (CSA) 4 - Dedicated serial lines The serial line must be highly immune to electromagnetic interference. Each ECU is thus associated with a resistance and capacity circuit condenser that filters out interference. Transmission protocol Circulation of transmission of data packages on serial lines is possible only if a transmission protocol is adopted. This is the set of rules that permits the exchange of data and commands between the various electronic units (control units or nodes). Each control unit is connected to its own serial line and is identified by a different address so that data package transfer is unequivocal. Data package transmission takes place from a transmitting control unit to another receiving control unit and is thus one-way. This operation involves the dispatch of a question package, which is followed by a response package. The information flow does not therefore involve a question/answer type exchange. Data packages The data package format (A) is unique but composed of two main parts: control (B) and outcome (C). A - Package B - Command: represents information sent by a control unit and contains a command and relevant data/parameters. C - Outcome: confirmation of reception and execution of the command by the control unit to which it is sent. T - Time within which the control unit sends the outcome. Command format A frame (1) consists of several blocks (2) or fields: 1 - Frame 2 - Block A - 1 byte identifies the start of data transmission B - address of the recipient control unit (ECU) is inserted C - address of the sending (transmitting) control unit (ECU) is inserted D - identifies control sent E - identifies control data F1- F2...Fn - sequence of all data associated with the control G - Checksum (CKS) The command part contains a set of information expressed in bytes, namely: Section A (HDR) is the first package byte and identifies the start of the transmission. - It is used to wake up and sychronise the high control units and prepare them to begin receiving data or information packages. Section B (DEST) or 'destination indicator' identifies the control unit for which the data package is destined. It is possible to identify up to 60 control units connected on the line: each control unit is allocated a different address so that the data package transfer is unique. Addresses are assigned by the network architecture. Section C (MITT) sending control unit address. Identifies the control unit that sends the command (i.e. transmitting ECU). Section D (CMD) data for transmission. Identifies the command sent on the serial line. Up to 255 different commands can be identified and sent via the network. The command list is set by the network architect. Section E (NBD) number of control data bytes. Identifies the number of bytes in the command (CMD) sent on the serial line. Each command may be associated with up to 255 bytes of data that make up the parameters. The values that may be assumed by each command are set by the network architect. Section F1-F2...FN, identifies the (NBD) sequence associated with the command. Section G (CKS) or CHECKSUM is a check to ensure the data package has been received correctly. It is calculated as the sum of all data package bytes (from HDR to FN) Once data package reception is complete, the control units send the outcome to the transmitting unit. The outcome can be: ACK = command acknowledged and done NACK = command not acknowledged NAP = command not applicable Outcome format Once the command has been received, the receiving control unit (ECU) must send the outcome (within a specific time T) to the transmitting control unit to terminate the data package exchange. Bit 7 Bit 6 Bit 5 Bit 4 Bit 3 Bit 2 Bit 1 Bit 0 ESI_1 ESI_0 ECU BIT 7, BIT 6 - Identifies the true outcome BIT 5, BIT 4, BIT 3 - BIT 2, BIT 1, BIT 0 - identifies the address of the destination control unit (ECU). The outcome information indicates:: If BIT 7 is at level = (0) and BIT 6 is at level = (0) the command is acknowledged and executed. (because the commands and data received are correct and can therefore be executed by the control unit because it is one of its commands). (ACK) Ifl BIT 7 is at level = (0) and BIT 6 is at level = (1) the command is not acknowledged (because the command data received are incorrect) (NACK) If the BIT 7 is at level = (1) andBIT 6 is at level = (0) the command is not applicable (because although it has been correctly received and although it can be executed by the control unit because it is one of its commands; it cannot be executed with the control unit (ECU) in its current status Or it is not one of its commands (NAP). The combination BIT 7 level (1) and BIT 6 level (1) is not permitted The other six bits (from BIT 6 to BIT 0) identify the address of the command destination control unit and can therefore address up to 63 units. Serial line status During operation, the serial line can assume two distinct statuses: FREE LINE: identifies serial line resting state or free state, i.e. no transmission on the line. In this condition, the ECU can start transmitting. LINE BUSY: a transmission is in progress on the line. In this condition, each ECU (with the exception of the sender) stands by until the data package transmission ends. Access to the line (conflict in transmission) Two or more control units can begin to send information at the same time. This simultaneous access can create a conflict on the line; during transmission, the control units therefore check that every individual byte in the data package has been correctly sent. In practice, they check to ensure that what they have sent is the the same as what they have read on the line. If the comparison is negative, a transmission conflict has occurred. The transmission conflict immediately interrupts the data package transmission. Under these conditions, the control units immediately abstain from occupying the line for a set time (programmed) to ensure that all the other control units record the data package interruption. Once this time has elapsed, the transmitting control units consider the line to be free again and gain access to transmission using the priority mechanism. Access with priority Each control unit is allocated a priority access code (Pa) which determines the circumstances under which the control units give up the line after recording a conflict. (The priority standard is established by the network architect). In practice, any control unit (node) that is preparing to transmit, expresses its intentions to the other control units (nodes) by means of an initial bit. If two control units (nodes) carry out this operation simultaneously they do not realise immediately but as soon as a transmitting control unit (node) detects a dominant symbol on the BUS, it immediately suspends transmission of messages with lower priority to make way for the control unit (node) that is sending the higher priority message. In practice, the higher priority message is sent via the network without any interruption or delay. The control unit (nodes) that were intending to send messages with lower priority naturally interrupt their transmissions and set themselves to receive before re-attempting to send when the transmission is complete. Because the dominant level is the lower level, small identifier numbers indicate high priority messages. Access to the line after a conflict obeys the following rules: The control unit waits for a given time (programmed) after the conflict and declares the line free.. Once the line is fere, the control unit waits for a further period determined by its priority code before gaining access to the line. The line free condition does not herald the start of transmission but activates access with priority and transmission therefore starts. The transmission is carried out firstly by the control unit with the highest priority, which takes control of the line to prevent a new conflict. The other control units with lower priority codes that generated the conflict therefore switch to listening mode. Once the data package has terminated, they can attempt to regain access to the line in order to transmit the previously interrupted data package. Transmission of a data package Example of data transmission. A - Package format B - Command: represents information sent by a control unit and contains a command and its parameter/data C - Outcome: confirmation of command reception and execution by the recipient control unit D - Free line T - Time (ms) within which the outcome must absolutely be sent Ta - time instant as a consequence of which a control unit with a higher access priority takes control of the line to prevent new conflict. Transmission of a data package between a transmitting control unit to the other control units connected to the network begins with the first byte (HDP) (this byte identifies the beginning and also wakes up the other control units at the beginning of package reception). It then continues with the command contents. Each control unit connected to the network swtiches to listening mode and determines, by means of the IND byte (address if the data package is addressed) At the end of command transmission, the receiving control unit processes it and transmits the outcoe. OUTCOME - YES/OUTCOME - NO If the control unit that permitted the command does not receive the outcome within the time required by the system, it considers that the command has not been sent and thus attempts to send the command again. It does not repeat the command if the outcome is received within the required time. A control unit in listening mode that identies a package not addressed to itself remains in listening mode until the end of data package transmission (i.e including outcome). The line is not occupied. The other control units consider the data package terminated when the time required for sending the outcome has elapsed. From that moment on, they can use the line to send new data packages.

COMPOSITION The starting system consists of the ignition switch operated by the key and the starter motor which is connected directly to the battery. In addition to tried and tested starter motors which are energized in series and in series/parallel, for some time now starter motors are being developed which are energized by ceramic, ferrite type permanent magnets. CIRCULAR SECTOR MAGNET WITH MAGNETICALLY PRE-ORIENTATED CRYSTALS The rough components are formed into the desired shape by pressing and extrusion. Finally, after a thorough baking process, the material produces the mangets which are black in colour with a ceramic structure. The magnetizing treatment takes place during the manufacturing process. The magnets have a circular section and replace the polar section and winding. 1 - Radial orientation 2 - Parallel orientation STATOR-INDUCTOR The positioning of the magnets cannot take place using strong compression or riveting, also because the magnets are fairly fragile: they are secured by flexible fastenings and springs and, in some cases, they are stuck to the casing. The casing can be compared to a simple mechanical component without wires and is fitted using two stay bolts; it is equipped with 6 magnetic poles. 1 - N-S permanent magnets ROTOR-ARMATURE The diagram below shows the rotor-armature assembly. 1 - Shaft 2 - Ring gear 3 - Satellite/planet gears 4 - Pinion/sun gear 5 - Armature 6 - Manifold/switch Given that the magnetic field is created by permanent magnets, the energizing is the same in all motor operating conditions; in addition, as there are no energizing windings, there is neither an energizing current nor ohmic resistance: the total resistance depends solely on the armature circuit. The rotation speed is only affected by the current which passes through the blades and reaches the rotor depending on the voltage. Since the motor is equipped with permanent magnets, i.e. with fixed polarity, the direction of rotation depends on how the current is sent to the blades. When the rotor rotates it transmits movement to the three satellite gears on special supports which transmit their torque to the ring gear on the output shaft where the pinion which rotates the flywheel can be found. The optimum reduction ratio 1:4.26 is 4.26 revolutions of the rotor for each revolution of the ring gear and the presence of the permanent magnets makes it possible to construct motors of equal power from a simple design which are small in size compared with motors which have windings. 1 - Pinion with free wheel 2 - Epicyclic reduction gear 3 - Rotor permanent mangets 4 - Complete polar casing 5 - Armature or rotor 6 - Blades 7 - Manifold 8 - Manifold side support 9 - Engagment relay 10 - Lever 11 - Control side support WIRING DIAGRAM The starter motor wiring diagram is illustrated below. 1 - Control unit on battery 2 - Starter motor 3 - Alternator 4 - Body computer 5 - Ignition switch 6 - Engine compartment control unit (CVM) 7- Control unit under dashboard (CPL)

COMPOSITION The alternator is a rotary machine which transforms mechanical energy into electrical energy. 1 - Rotor electro-magnetic circuit 2 - Assembly rods 3 - Rectifier side support 4 - Negative heat dissipation plate 5 - Positive heat dissipation plate 6 - Zener type pressfit power diode 7 - Manifold 8 - Regulation unit 9 - Heat shield cap 10 - Rectifier side bearing 11 - Rectifier side inner fan 12 - Stator electronic circuit 13 - Control side support 14 - Control side inner fan 15 - Control side bearing Like all electric machines, it basically consists of two parts: a rotor and a stator. The diagram below shows the rotor for an alternator with internal ventilation. Rotor The rotor is composed of a cylindrical magnetic core, concentric to the drive shaft, which has a toroid coil and two opposing magnetic impellers which are magnetized by the winding in the actual core. The impellers have six, claw-shaped, poles each, which interpolate reciprocally so that there are alternately six North poles and six South poles. There is therefore a single rotor winding which produces the e.m.f. for all the partial magnetic circuits. Stator The diagram below illustrates the stator. 1 - Star conection stator 2 - Triangular connection stator Stator This consists of a ring-shaped laminated group joined by two or more axial welding seams on the outside. It usually has thirty six grooves which contain the three-phase winding made from insulated copper wire with vinyl acetate and is connected, as necessary, by a star or triangular connection. RECTIFIER BRIDGE The diagram shows the rectifier bridge. 1 - Zener type power diode 2 - Dissipation plate 3 - Terminal B + alternator Bridge specifications The bridge consists of: Zener press-fit diodes. Diodes fitted on the dissipation plates electrically connected to the connection terminals with the phases. Dissipation plates. Large size dissipators. Phase insulation until the connection with the bridge through a rubber cable loom. Excess voltage limitation if the '+ battery' loads are disconnected guaranteed by the zener diodes. 1 - Normal diode 2 - Zener diode Zener diodes If the diodes are polarized directly they both allow the current to pass from the anode to the cathode (V+ I+): a zener diode therefore behaves like a normal silicon diode. If polarized inversely, initially the current does not flow from the cathode to the anode up to Vz (V-I-). Beyond Vz a normal diode is ruined, but a zener diode, on the other hand, continues to work normally because its resistance in these conditions decreases sharply. A zener diode is therefore a voltage stabilizer diode. On cars the voltage ranges from 4.7 to 24 Volt. It is one of the most important components in the regulation unit. It is often used for protection against polarity inversion or excess voltage. SPECIFCATIONS ALTERNATOR WITH INTERNAL VENTILATION SPECIFICATIONS The main feature of this type of alternator, with a 115 mm diameter stator, is having dual internal ventilation with the vanes inclined to guarantee the maximum flow of air and, at the same time, limit noise. Alternators with internal ventilation, for the same power supply, are smaller and lighter than types with external ventilation and satisfy all current application requirements (space in engine compartments is always at a premium). In addition to this, in terms of quality, these alternators are more reliable and durable than the best the competition currently has to offer on the market. In depth studies and research have made it possible to introduce all the devices, in production, designed to limit the noise produced by various components (fluid dynamics, mangetic, mechanical). Wiring diagram The diagram shows the A127-IR-14V-120A alternator. 1- Alternator 2 - Interference condenser 3 - Regulation unit 4 - Energizing rotor 5 - Electric field stator 6 - Zener diode rectifier bridge 7 - Alternator recharging warning light in panel 12V-1.2 - 3.4 W 8 - Body computer 9 - CAN network information OPERATION With the alternator not working and the ignition key in the ON position, the body computer lights up the warning light in the instrument panel (NQS) and sends a power supply to the voltage regulator incorporated in the actual alternator via terminal D+. In these conditions the energizing circuit (rotor) is enabled to earth by the regulator electronics. With the alternator rotating through the effect of the alteration in the number of revs and the mangetic field, a three-phase alternating volage is produced in the electrical circuit (stator) which, rectified by the diode bridge, can come out of terminal B+. When the upper fixed calibration level is reached (13.7 - 14.2 V) the battery is charged and the system supplied. The body computer checks the efficiency of the alternator recharging system by measuring two parameters: the voltage signal coming from alternator terminal D+ and the engine rpm signal received at the CAN network from the injection control unit (NCM). The lighting up of the warning light in the instrument panel (NQS) is determined by the levels recognized by the body computer being exceeded: in practice, if the voltage is too high (> 16.5 ± 0.5 V) or if the voltage is too low (< 7 ± 0.5 V) this causes the alternator to work irregularly in both cases with a consequent instruction by the NBC to light up the warning light in the instrument panel. If recharging signals are not present or irregular, carry out the following checks before dismantling the alternator: check belt tension; check the nut on the positive alternator terminal (B+) is tight and ensure the washer is present; check the nut on the excitation terminal (D+) is tight and ensure the washer is present; check that the nuts on the positive junction unit in the engine bay are tight; check the bolts securing the negative terminal to the body are tight; check the battery terminals are clean and fully tight; If the Body Computer does not provide the energizing signal, the alternator is energized at 1000 engine rpm (about 2200 alternator rpm) exploiting the residual magnetic field.

COMPOSITION The current generation system consists of: the alternator; the battery; the recharging warning light in the instrument panel; the ignition switch for the system connections. BATTERY The main features of batteries used on new models are the mounting plates made from active materials produced through the calcium lead production technology which has replaced the older antimony- lead type. This involves a mechanical stretching process for a continuous lead band to reach the final productio of a grille covered in lead oxides for the positive poles and metallic lead only for the negative poles, instead of the use of casting machines to produce grilles for fusion. The use of a material such as lead-calcium-tin alloy guarantees a considerable reduction in the electrolysis during the operation of the accumulator (dissociation of the water into its components of hydrogen and oxygen) where the gases can escape resulting in reduced evaporation of the actual water with a drastic reduction in the maintenance required for this type of battery. 1 - Cover 2 - Cap edge 3 - Positive plate 4 - Negative plate 5 - Separator 6 - Bridges 7 - Electrolyte 8 - Water gauge 9 - Negative pole 10 - Monobloc 11 - Maximum electrolyte level 12- Minimum electrolyte level 13 - Dipstick 14 - Cap Battery electrical specifications: Lead accumulator, low maintenance type. Cover: EURODIN with ramp type sealing elements on cover; press-fit caps (one cap per element) with protection system against fluid penetration from the outside. Gas evacuation through caps with gas/liquid separation system Cover seal: heat welding. Attachment to the base: joined on four sides. Poles: lead bushes produced through cold-pressing with sealing labyrinth in the press-work area on the cover. Electrolyte level check: through the openings in the caps in the cover, checking the consistency between the indicator (dipstick) and the electrolyte level. The dipstick indicates the max. level allowed, therefore the electrolyte should just come into contact with the lower end of the dipstick. The min. level is reached when the electrolyte exceeds the top end of the separators and/or plates by 10 mm. Water gauge for checking min. electrolyte level and battery charge. No. of plates: 6 positive + 5 negative. Alloy grille: lead-calcium-tin. Separator thickness: 1.15 mm. Plate thickness: positive 1.80 mm; negative 1.60 Electrolyte density: 1280 ± 10 g/dm3 at 25°C with battery 100% charged. Electrolyte density at 25° Celsius: 1280 g/litre 100 % of charge 1240 g/litre 75 % of charge 1200 g/litre 50 % of charge 1160 g/litre 25 % of charge 1120 g/litre drained 1110 g/litre totally drained. Control system This battery has an indicator for checking the battery which is a water gauge which makes it possible to qualitatively monitor the level of the electrolyte and the battery charge; this also allows the Customer to initially check the efficiency of the battery. this also allows the Customer to initially check the efficiency of the battery. This device consists of a transparent plexiglas cylinder: one end contains an indicator fixed to the battery cover; on the other end there is a drip tray, made from an acid-resistant material, drilled in such a way to allow the battery electrolyte to come into contact with a green coloured ball which is housed in the drip tray and can slide along a plane inclined towards the centre of the area of the cylinder. Water gauge Two types of information are provided; electrolyte level; battery charge. 1 - Cylinder 2 - Indicator 3 - Drip tray 4 - Ball Operation The operating principle of this device is based on the contact between the drip tray and the battery fluid. The ball has been designed in such a way that, at a given electrolyte density value, it rises along an inclined plane and reaches the transparent surface of the indicator, colouring the centre of this area green: CONDITION 1. When the density of the electrolyte decreases (battery run down), the ball moves from the centre and the light is subject to refraction to the extent that the colour in the centre of the indicator darkens: CONDITION 2. When the fluid no longer bathes the cylinder casing, the ball descends completely and the area in the centre appears even lighter: CONDITION 3. 1 - Condition 1 2 - Condition 2 3 - Condition 3 To sum up, the colour of the indicator reflects the state of the battery charge as set out in the table below. CONDITION 1 CONDITION 2 CONDITION 3 Information visible Dark colour with green area in the centre Dark colour with green area in the centre Light, bright colour Electrolyte level Correct Correct Below minimum State of charge from 55% to 100% Battery discharged Indeterminate Action to undertake No action Recharge the battery Top up electrolyte with distilled water This device: does not give readings concerning a possible internal short circuit; the density of the electrolyte varies with the temperature; a prolonged stop could halt the mixing process of the reagents and thereby lead to a measurement which could refer to the surface layers only. if the electrolyte level is low then there are no reliable readings. To sump up the approximation of the measurement is around 15% (battery charge indicator calibration = 70% ± 15%). As a result of this reading error, it is necessary to check the battery charge more accurately in a Service Situation. Cap In low maintenance type batteries with lead-calcium-tin elements the seal is guaranteed by the press-fit caps with an anti-penetration system with a gas evacuation device through the actual caps. The caps which allow the escape of the gases produced in the battery prevent the leakage of liquid. The cap consists of: The cap casing: it acts as to prevent liquids escaping, but allows gas to escape through special openings. The labyrinth: it prevents the particles which are released during the operation of the battery from obstructing the special diaphragm. The semi-pervious diaphragm: thanks to a special layer of PTFE (poly-tetra-fluoro-ethylene) it prevents the escape of liquid, allowing the gases which are produced during the normal operation of the battery to pass through. 1 - Cap casing 2 - Labyrinth 3 - Diaphragm Battery discharge in rest conditions Correct battery dimensions for model / trim level have been calculated to take into account power uptake when the ignition is switched off. This absorption should not exceed 0.6 mA for each Ah of battery capacity; this is to ensure that, if the vehicle has been left for one month with all the consumers not controlled by the ignition switched on, residual battery capacity is half of nominal capacity, i.e. enough charge is left to start up the engine under normal environmental temperature conditions. In the Max Level maximum condition (11), the electrolyte should barely come into contact with the lower end of the dipstick (3), positioned inside the battery and visible through the openings in the cover in each cell producing the so-called 'meniscus effect'. The operations of checking the electrolyte level and, if necessary, topping it up through the individual battery cell openings, should not be carried out by the Customer, but by trained Network personnel as part of the Planned Maintenance Programme every 20,000 km. SPECIFCATIONS GAS DISCHARGE HEADLAMPS Introduction The lights play an important role among the vehicle's active safety systems. The need to improve the performance of current systems, based on halogen lamps, in terms of light energy emitted, spectral range and bulb duration has led to the technological development of gas discharge headlamps and the relevant devices which permit their operation on the vehicle. Three main advantages have resulted from the development of this technology: more efficient brightness permits a reduction in electrical energy when in steady state; the high light emission allows the size of the lights cluster to be reduced (particularly the height) offering greater freedom of design of the front; on average, the life is double that of a halogen bulb. The gas discharge headlamp technology has led to the development of a set of devices which, in short, comprise: xenon bulb; reflecting surface of the headlamp; control electronics, consisting of a reactor (igniter) and control unit (ballast); automatic light beam adjustment Light beam (isolux curve) of conventional headlamp Light beam (isolux curve) of discharge headlamp COMPLETE LIGHTS CLUSTER Each lights cluster contains the components necessary for the operation of the discharge lamp (bulb, reactor, control unit, control motor); the conventional components are also present (side lights, direction indicators, fog lights, main beam). Cross section of headlamp showing the gas discharge bulb 1 - Main beam 2 - Side light 3 - Gas discharge bulb 4 - Fog light bulb XENON LAMP The xenon lamp comprises a bulb containing two electrodes a few millimetres apart, and filled with xenon gas at low pressure. The emission of light is brought about by the striking up of an arc between the two electrodes, which is maintained during the operation of the bulb; this process is similar to what happens in neon tubes in civil applications. Unlike neon tubes, however, in an automobile application, however, it is unthinkable to have to wait for some minutes before the process stabilises, so the lights cluster has an electronic control device which permits operation, with regard to warm-up time, comparable to conventional headlamps. REFLECTIVE SURFACE The xenon bulb requires a new reflective surface, as the light emission point is shaped and positioned differently compared to the halogen bulb. The reflector used is of the complex surface type, so with no spherical lens. This surface receives light beams coming from the bulb and orientates them so as to provide a correct light beam distribution. Control electronics Each bulb is controlled by electronics consisting of two devices: the control unit (ballast) and ignition reactor (igniter). The purpose of the ballast is to convert the low-voltage direct current coming from the vehicle's battery into medium-voltage alternating current, and to control the subsystem's operation in closed loop. The ballast is thus able to control in an optimum way the characteristic voltage-current in the ignition stage, and can deliver to the bulb the power required to for operation in steady state. The igniter is controlled by the ballast and can generate the high voltage (max 25 kV) necessary for striking up the arc between the electrodes. The ballast in the left headlamp acts as 'MASTER': it receives the signals from the sensors, processes them and re-transmits them also the ballast of the right 'SLAVE' headlamp. Wiring diagram The figure shows a general diagram of the electrical connections A, MASTER headlamp B, SLAVE headlamp Sa, Front sensor Sb, Rear sensor DIA, Diagnostic socket Operation The operation of a xenon bulb is divided into four phases Ignition In this stage, the ballast generates a voltage which can strike up a specific device located in the igniter. A voltage step-up circuit transfers the overvoltage, suitably amplified, to the lamp, thus causing a discharge between the electrodes. Maintaining the arc (take-over) During this stage (a few seconds), the bulb is supplied with extra power which is necessary to cause the rapid evaporation of the metallic halides contained in the bulb, so as to quickly reach the brightness steady state. Under these conditions, the lamp emits a flash of light of double the normal intensity for a period of about 100 microseconds. Warm-up For a period of about two minutes, the ballast regulates the light intensity by measuring the physical state of the bulb from its impedance characteristics (closed-loop check). Steady state The light beam is continuously checked in closed loop even in steady state conditions. 1 - Supply (12 V) 2 - High-voltage generator 3 - Square-wave generator 4 - CPU 5 - Voltage step-up circuit A. Ballast B. Igniter C. Bulb Automatic headlamp alignment adjuster Because of the brightness of the beam emitted by the bulb, the vehicle must have an automatic headlamp alignment adjuster to avoid dazzling oncoming vehicles because of changes in alignment. The device intervenes in certain conditions: static type, due to load distribution; dynamic type, due to acceleration and deceleration. The automatic adjuster also ensures greater driving comfort, as the lit area remains stable and the eye does not have to constantly adapt to variations in illumination. The device comprises: a stepper motor for each headlamp; two load sensors, connected to the front and rear suspension, right side. Adjustment This is achieved via the signal of the load sensors which, connected to the suspension, give an indication of the vehicle's load condition. The control unit is 'activated' whenever the ignition is turned ONand resets the headlamps to the corrrect hight (calculated in relation to the vehicle load), which consists of the full tilting and subsequent positioning of the reflector. The signals of the load sensors are periodically acquired and suitably averaged so as to proceed, if necessary, with an adjustment of the headlamp position (e.g. fuel consumption during driving). This adjustment is not immediate, but is filtered over time to avoid unwanted adjustments (e.g. potholes, rough road surface, etc.). This adjustment is also carried out when the lights are off, so that the beam is correctly positioned the moment when the lights are switched on. Load sensors The sensors are fixed to the vehicle body, while an appropriately shaped lever follows the movement of the suspension. The sensor is supplied by the headlamp control unit, and supplies as an output a linear signal proportional to the position of the suspension in relation to the body. A - Part secured to the body B - Part secured to the suspension lever a - Angle of inclination of the lever V - Voltage of sensor's output signal Adjustment actuator A stepper actuator inside the lights cluster carries out the adjustment. This consists of a stepper motor and a screw-nutscrew reduction gear, which transforms from rotary into linear the motion of a pushrod hinged via a spherical ball to the reflective surface. 1 - Stepper motor 2 - Manual headlamp adjuster Self-diagnosis The electronics which manage the system include a self-test function which continuously checks its operation. The control unit carries out a continuous autodiagnosis of the system operation. In particular, it detects and memorises any faults. Faults stored in the control unit memory can be analysed by the Examiner or other diagnostic instruments. Recovery The self-test management logic also has the 'recovery' function: if errors are detected, the system no longer works correctly, and so incorrect orientation of the light beam could dangerously dazzle other vehicles. The light beam is then positioned low so it cannot dazzle under any circumstances, but permits sufficient illumination for safe driving to a garage on the Service Network. Zeroing In the case of replacement of a component in the system (headlamp, sensor, etc.), it is necessary to connect up the diagnostic instruments and carry out a self-learning procedure, to automatically reset the system, which must recognise the headlamp correctly algined position (position '0') from which it must make the appropriate adjustments.

The activation signal is given by pressing the centre section of the steering wheel by the spokes. COMPOSITION View of horn assembly 1 - Horns 2 - Mounting bracket The two horns which make up the unit have different sounding tones, one has a high tone, the other a low tone. The two horns are connected to the electrical system by means of single-pole contacts. OPERATION The pressure exerted on the centre of the steering wheel causes the compressino of one of the three springs, near the bolts fixing the Air Bag module (see Subassembly 5580C) which closes the circuit to earth. View of horn control circuit 1 - Spring 2 - Printed circuit 3 - Horn connection 4 - Interconnection casing The three springs form part of a printed circuit, in the partition housing the Air Bag module (see Subassembly 5580C) which ends with a two-way connection. The connecting bridge for the horns comes out of the interconnection casing, at the base of the housing. The casing is, in turn, connected, via an eight-way connector, to the bridge which comes out of the clock spring. The connection to the system, via the clock spring, allows the rotation of the steering wheel, ensuring the correct transmission of the various signals, without the aid of sliding contacts. CLOCK SPRING On versions without radio controls on the steering, on the side the clock spring is fixed to the steering column switch unit it has two connection points, one for the horn signal and one for the connection to the Air Bag module whilst on versions with radio/telephone and Selespeed controls on the steering wheel the connection is achieved via a single twelve-way connector. SPECIFICATIONS INTRODUCTION The instrument panel is inside the B-CAN and is called the NQS (Instrument Panel Node). The signals concerned with systems on the C-CAN are made available to the NQS by the Body Computer Node via an interface known as a Gateway. The task of the NQS is to display the vehicle operating parameters and to notify the driver of any possible faults in the on-board electronic systems. The instrument panel includes a TN LCD display and a reconfigurable DSTN dot-matrix display (HIGH version). OPERATION The task of the instrument panel node is to: Receive and transmit information on the B-CAN Manage the accessory functions. Receive and manage signals not from network Display the vehicle operating statuses The diagram below illustrates the main Instrument Panel Node connections The functions involving the Instrument Panel Node are listed below: SPEEDOMETER The instrument panel receives speed information, expressed in km/h, via the B-CAN line and then displays it by means of a pointer which is moved by a step motor. The speed information comes from the NBC and the latter calculates the speed using the wheel rpm signal from the NFR (ABS) and measurement of the wheel circumference memorized in the NBC The pointer remains stationary, in the rest position, at speeds of between 0 and 4 km/h. The speed signal received is shown at higher speeds. Error conditions In case of error, the speedometer pointer will position itself on the zero speed notch (rest position) and remain in this position for as long as the fault persists. Speed limit (only high version) It is possible set a speed limit from the Menu, with a range from 30 to 250 km/h Limit selection is closed loop (not rolling: reach limit and go back). When the selection has been made and the function is active, if vehicle speed exceeds the preset limit of +1 km/h, the matrix display shows a + symbol warning message and an acoustic signal is activated (Alarm beep 1). The alarm signal remains active (message up to 20s, afterwards only the symbol) as long as the speed is lower than 5 km/h below the alarm activation speed. EXAMPLE If a limit of 170 km/h is selected, the signal (message + symbol + alarm beep) is activated at speeds equal to 171 km/h and deactivated at vehicle speeds equal to 166 km/h. ODOMETER The display contains 7 segments and is configured as a quasi dot matrix to obtain a dot matrix-like configuration. The panel receives information, from the B-CAN line, on the distance travelled processed by the NBC using information coming from the NFR and it increases the total milometer and trip meter counters. The km travelled are shown on an LCD display (1) that shows headlamp alignment adjustment information. The display lighting is green and there is an SMD LED. The LCD has 6 digits (with 7 segments for each digit) for the total reading and 4 digits plus a decimal point for the trip reading. Insignificant zeros are not displayed in order to reduce the numbers shown to the important ones only. When the "0 km" key is pressed (outside the NQS) for longer than 1s < t < 3 s the partial odometer is reset, but not the total odometer, the distance travelled (Trip) or the Service mileage. The instrument memorizes the total mileage so that if the battery is disconnected (+30) not more than +/1 km is lost whilst the trip meter memory is lost altogether. When the instrument with LCD odometer is delivered to the assembly factory the milometer can only be zeroed once within the first 200 km (or 125 miles). The possibility of carrying out this zeroing is indicated on the LCD by the letter "H" at the first digit (with 7 segments) on the left of the milometer. If the above operation is carried out before reaching 200 km, the total odometer resets to zero (the partial odometer reesets, the trip counter resets and the Service mileage resets) by pressing the "0 km" key for time t > 10 s and the letter H disappears. If this operation is not carried out, when 200 km is reached/exceeded, the letter H disappears and the mileage is displayed with no possiblity of zeroing the milometer any more. The instrument allows the programming of the total number of km (if it is replaced) on condition that the figure entered is higher than the last value memorized When the maximum mileage is reached on the milometer (699999 km - 399999 miles), it is not zeroed but horizontal bars/dashes are displayed. When the trip meter reaches 999.9 Km, it returns to 0.0 Behaviour of mileometer with the key out With the ignition switched off, nothing is shown on the display; in this case the "0km" key has no function, when one of the front doors (left/right) is opened/closed the milometer will light up and display the trip meter and total mileage information for a certain time. Error conditions In case of error, the odometer displays the last valid value until it receives a new valid value. REV COUNTER The panel receives rpm information supplied to the network by the NCM via the B-CAN line and displays it by means of a pointer moved by a step motor. The panel processes the engine rpm data without corrections applying a time constant of 200 ms so that the response to the zero RPM - full scale defection RPM step is less than 2 seconds Pointer position at key-off At key-off, the pointer is set to 0 (0 rpm). Examples of errors In case of error, the pointer sets itself to ZERO (beginning of scale) until the error status disappears. Alarm signals If the pointer reaches the red danger area, if partial panel lighting has been set, it is adjusted to the required level using the dimmer. Engine coolant temperature gauge The temperature reading allows values between +50 and +130 to be displayed The panel receives engine temperature information, via the B-CAN line, made available by the NCM, which varies between an actual temperature range of -40 to +215 °C (the range displayed is from +50 to +130) and the NQS displays the temperature by means of a pointer moved by a stepping motor. Pointer movements are uniform. Gauge/warning light behaviour at the key-on Ton = Temperature reading at key-on. Toff = Temperature reading corresponding to the gauge position at the key-off (which usually corresponds to the actual temperature reading at the key-off). If what is defined in condition "d" takes place (burst of heat: 2 mins inhibition) the temperature reading corresponding to the position of the gauge is different from the actual temperature of the engine coolant. The temperature reading is always guaranteed even in electrical operating limit conditions (9/16V). If the operating voltage is not stable then the frequency acquisition for the temperature signal allows a correct reading on the panel. Operating logic for the engine coolant temperature gauge at the key-on. I = Gauge position T = Time (s) t1 = 1.5 s + 0.5 / -0 t2 = 3s t1+t2 = 5s max. Pointer behaviour at key-off: Under conditions of key-off, the pointer moves to the zero notch. Temperature warning light and indicator operating logic Operating logic for engine coolant temperature gauge in normal operating conditions I = Scale reading T = Temperature A - Gauge operation by instrument panel B - Warning light operation by c.c.m. C - Start of scale D - Centre of scale E - Start of red sector F - End of scale For temperatures of T = 50 °C, the pointer should be at the first reference on the scale (start of scale). For temperatures between 50 ÷ 80 °C the pointer should increase in a linear fashion. For temperatures between 80 ÷ 100 °C (normal operation), the pointer should remain in a stable position in the centre of the scale. For temperatures between 100 ÷ 120 °C (uphill) and between 115 ÷ 100 °C (downhill) the pointer should move in a linear fashion. For temperatures of T = 120 ± 1 °C, the pointer should be located at the beginning of the red sector of the scale. For temperatures of T = 122 °C the pointer should reach the position corresponding to the beginning of the red sector and, as soon as the engine management control unit sends the warning light on signal, it should be positioned at the end of the scale (t = 1 s); the engine coolant temperature overheating warning light should come on at the same time. In addition: if the warning light on signal coming from the c.c.m. remains in the ON state, the pointer should remain at the end of the scale and the warning light should remain on; if the c.c.m sends the warning light off signal (when the temperature goes below the level usually equal to T = 115 ± 1°C), the instrument panel should instantly switch the coolant overheating warning light off and the pointer should place itself (t = 1 s) in the position corresponding to the (actual) temperature value measured. There is a hysteresis of 5 °C, in other words, for example, the warning light is switched on at 120°C, it is switched off at 115 °C. Engine coolant overheating warning light The panel receives the information that the warning light is switched on/off via the B-CAN line. The software strategy that regulates the switching on/off of the engine coolant overheating warning light and the operation of the pointer in the end of scale position when the temperature levels/limits are reached, both in normal operation and if there is a burst of heat, is contained inside the engine management control unit. Error conditions/diagnosis The instrument panel warning light is activated at each key-on (check stage); after 4 secs. the CCM/NCM sends the panel the command to switch the warning light off. During this check stage the behaviour of the gauge should be as defined in the previous paragraph ("gauge behaviour at key-on"). Through the effect of the warning light coming on, the pointer is not in the end of scale position during the check stage. If the warning light on conditions were present at the key-on (engine coolant temperature overheating and warning light already on at the previous key-off), the c.c.m. keeps the command to switch the warning light on activated and the instrument panel continues to keep the warning light in an ON state and places the pointer in the end of scale position. DIAGNOSIS OF CONNECTING LINE WITH TEMPERATURE SENSOR The system checks for the presence of irregular system conditions. Therefore if there is a faulty connection between the temperature sensor and the NCM, the latter commands the "injection/EOBD failure" warning light in the NQS to come on. 1 - Instrument panel 2 - Engine Management Node 3 - Sensor If there is a fault, the engine coolant temperature gauge pointer should be on the zero reference (rest position) and should remain in that position as long as the fault persists. Indicator recovery logic (step motor) If the indicator stepping motors are losing steps, due, for example, to: transportation/movement, installation of the panel on the vehicle or as a result of serious mechanical and electro-magnetic stresses that have occurred whilst the vehicle was being driven on the road or whilst it was stationary. There is a "return to zero" logic for all the gauges (partial or complete recovery) at each key-on and key-off operation This logic also provides for the "return to zero" of all the gauges (complete recovery) each time the battery is connected (+BATT.) When the gauges are in the "normal operating" positions, this logic guarantees that any movements/fluctuations of the gauges are not visible to the user. ENGINE OIL LEVEL gauge (only for JTD engine) The engine oil level gauge function indicates engine oil level at start-up on the instrument display. The gauge is equipped with a special circuit that controls a hot wire oil level sensor. The information is displayed: on the display (odometer) on the LOW version, on the reconfigurable matrix display on the HIGH version. Display of the signal LOW VERSION At key on, the message OIL is displayed on the lower part of the odometer for 10 seconds. Six digital squares on the upper part of the display gradually light up to show the amount of oil present in the engine. With al the squares lit, the oil level is at maximum. As the oil level drops, the squares in the upper part gradually go out. When the oil level is at minimum, the squares in the upper part are all out and the underlying dashes flash at a rate of 0.5 Hz. If the oil level is higher than a critical value, above the maximum level, the message “HIGH OIL” is displayed for 10 seconds. If a break or short-circuit is present in the indicator circuit at key-on, the word OIL flashes for 10 second at a rate of 0.5 Hz and the dashes disappear. HIGH VERSION At key on, the message engine oil level is displayed for 10 seconds. The amount of oil present in the engine is displayed by turning six bars on/off. The maximum oil level is represented by all the bars lit. If the oil level is lower than the minimum specified level, the bars are all off and the message "minimum oil level" is displayed for 10 seconds. The bars are also all empty and the low oil level symbol appears in the warning light area. If the oil level is above the maximum specified level, the bars will all be lit up and the "maximum oil level" message will be displayed for 10 secs. If a fault is detected in the oil level sensor, the "oil level sensor fault" message will be displayed for 10 seconds. Signal acquisition The vehicle must be level for accurate signal acquisition. The barycentric position of the sensor nevertheless compensates for minor tilting of the vehicle. The counter is zeroed the first time the battery is connected. At the first key on, the oil level is ready (reading time equal to 1 second) and the result is shown on the display. Afte reading, the counter is set to 20 minutes. During the key on period, the counter decreases by one unit per minute to a minimum value of 2 minutes. At the next key off, the counter decreases from two down to zero. At the next key on, and only if the counter is equal to zero, the system reads and stores the new value. If the counter is still >0 at key on, it is compared with the previous reading and if: the current reading is greater than or equal to the previous reading by 3 segments, measurement display notches, the reading is downloaded, stored and the counter is reset to 20 and the countdown starts again as before; the current reading is less than 3 segments, measurement display notches, the reading is not stored and the level status corresponding to the last effective reading is displayed. The counter resets itself to 20 and begins the countdown again. Engine OIL TEMPERATURE GAUGE (only for 3.2 V6) The function displays the oil temperature, directly acquired from the guage by means of a sensor, and also displays an excessive temperature warning on the display. The information is shown on the reconfigurable matrix display The engine oil temperature is downloaded by means of an analogue input and then displayed on a bar chart: 0 Bars: Temperature between -40ºC and 60ºC 1 Bar: Temperature between 60ºC and 80ºC 2 Bars: Temperature between 80ºC and 100ºC 3 Bars: Temperature between 100ºC and 120ºC 4 Bars: Temperature between 120ºC and 140ºC 5 Bars: Temperature greater than 140ºC Activation/deactivation of each bar graph element is managed by a hysteresis operating logic that prevents the image from becoming unstable. WARNING LIGHTS Specifications The warning lights can be switched on or off by the NQS via a command from the B-CAN, for the systems that are connected to the C-CAN the messages are made available at the B-CAN via the NBC gateway or for the direct management of the component connected to the NQS. The warning lights usually come on when there is a fault, but some warning lights also come on at the key-on for less than 4 secs. to indicate the check on the system to which they are connected. On the HIGH VERSION some warning lights are turned on during the check stage while on the LOW version, they are not turned on at key-on but only in the case of a fault. Smart warning lights are only used for the AIR BAG system failure warning light. The circuit is as follows: A = Towards the control unit Operation Minimum engine oil pressure The display takes place by means of a symbol on the dot matrix (HIGH) or a LED (LOW). IGNITION The warning light is turned on only if the event (fault onset) occurs by a command from the NCM and for 1.5 seconds if the engine rpm is greater than 700 rpm. SWITCHING OFF When the message is received from the NCM, if the NQS is disconnected from the B-CAN network and if the engine rpm is lower than 200 rpm. Alternator failure The information is displayed by means of a symbol on the dot matrix (HIGH) or a LED (LOW). IGNITION The warning light is turned on only if the event (fault onset) occurs by a command from the NBC and for 1.5 seconds if the engine rpm is greater than 550 rpm. SWITCHING OFF When the message is received from the NBC, if the NQS is disconnected from the B-CAN network and if the engine rpm is lower than 200 rpm. Engine control (eobd) fault The information is displayed by means of a symbol lit by an LED on the HIGH version. The symbol is also shown on the dot matrix if a fault is present. The NCM is connected directly to the NQS IGNITION The warning light is controlled directly by the NCM (direct connection between the NQS and the NCM). On the HIGH version only, if the symbol is repeated on the DOT matrix for 1.5 seconds upon receipt of the fault command and if the engine rpm number is greater than 700 rpm. SWITCHING OFF The warning light is controlled directly by the NCM (direct connection between the NQS and the NCM). On the HIGH version, the symbol is repeated on the dot matrix when the fault cessation command is received The EOBD (European On Board Diagnosis) system continuously diagnoses emission-related components on the vehicle and turns on a warning light on the control panel to indicate any deterioration in the components. The aim of the system is to: monitor system efficiency; indicate an increase in emissions due to vehicle malfunction; indicate the need to replace damaged components. Timely intervention to repair the fault that caused the warning light to come on is an obligation that depends on the laws and Highway Code in the country where the car is driven.
